THE POEM IN HĀʾ:
Why does my soul prolong its complaint to creatures, while it hopes for God?
Its complaint corrupts its sincerity — that is what alarmed it and destroyed it.
Had it drawn near to its King and purified its love for Him, He would have brought it near.
But it preferred His creatures over Him, out of ignorance of Him, so He distanced it.
It made itself poor to creatures; had it fled to Him instead of them, He would have enriched it.
It complains to His creation, as if they owned its benefit and harm.
Had it delegated its affair to its Creator and made its truthfulness sound, and relied on Him,
He would have exchanged its worries for relief and would not leave it in prolonged grief.
It angers Him for the pleasure of His creatures — woe to it, how great is its trial!
Had it angered the servants and pleased its Lord, He would have pleased it.
I have a soul that I love to describe, that you may know its description and its names.
So hear my attributes of it, that perhaps the possessor of understanding may grasp the secret of its meaning.
It strives toward frivolity, and that is its goal — woe to it, how harmful is its striving!
I rebuke it, and it disobeys me, as if I were not among those who love it.
It looks at the faults of others foolishly — and how many faults of its own it forgets!
It has wronged me by its evil companionship, and left me neither piety nor standing.
Much idle talk in its gatherings, little remembrance in its prayer-place.
Little gratitude at its blessings, weak patience at its trials.
Slow to pursue its interests, swift to run into its calamities.
Much deferral in its promises, lying in all its claims.
Clear-sighted toward passion and its temptation, blind to matters beyond it.
Energetic at the time of its pleasure, lazy at the time of its remembrance.
Sleepy of eye toward the worship of Him who perfected its formation and proportioned it.
Much security in its health, great fear in its harm.
Companion of pride and hypocrisy — indeed, its pride has corrupted it and made it transgress.
Great in praise and commendation of one who raises its rank and abode.
Prolonging blame and ugliness toward one who knows its measure and its transgression.
It rejoices in its eating and drinking, and its face is set toward sleep, which entices it.
It remembers the faults of creatures, forgetting what its own ingratitude has wrought.
How far between my soul and the soul of a youth whom piety purified and cleansed!
Knowledge taught it its guidance and gave it insight, then nourished it with lawful strength.
It stood it in the darkness on its feet, and its eyes poured with tears.
When it desired a passion, it returned it, by fear of its worshipped One, and it desisted.
It disciplined it with fasting, and it was subdued, willy-nilly, from its error and its enticement.
Mindful of God, thankful, sincere in its secret and its whispered prayer.
For God is a soul, divinely guided, that sought refuge in its Lord, and He sheltered it.
Her Lord honored it and ennobled it, and from the waters of certainty He watered it.
It ascended to Him by its good reflection, then by the purity of its love He purified it.
That one, if it calls for its need, He answers it swiftly and responds.
If it is tried by calamities, it is patient; or if it asks what it wills, He gives it.
It is not like my soul, which is disobedient — I command it earnestly and forbid it.
Yet it disobeys the Command of God — woe to me for what it has wrought, and woe to it!
How can it return to its Lord when it has submitted to its Satan, who has enticed it?
Whenever I say: "O soul, be rebuked, and fear God in your affairs,"
It is silent toward the truth while hearing it, as if I did not intend it.
Had it known something of what it was created for, its knowledge would grieve it and make it weep.
Had it known God with true knowledge, it would have made right its piety and its God-fearing.
But its ignorance of its Creator has made it heedless of its guidance and distracted it.
Woe to my soul — and woe is truly due to it — if its Lord turns it away and destroys it!
The pleasure of life deceives it, and it does not know what its end will be.
I have become straitened by it, and I imprison it; I would not disobey God were it not for it.
If I attempt obedience, it slackens and shows estrangement and reluctance.
I have become at war with the soul; it commands me to passion, and I forbid it.
We are like two horns in a battle; I don the armor of patience when I meet it.
It confronts me with the hosts of passion — and what patience can endure its onslaught?
If I am cowardly in battle, it emboldens me; or if my strength weakens in the encounter,
I throw it down sometimes, and it throws me down — but it has the precedence when I meet it.
I love it, yet it is my enemy, as if I were not among those who love it.
An enemy I cannot hate — would that I could forget it!
It swims in the seas of its temptation, kneeling in the veils of its darkness.
I think that if it refuses my compliance, it loses its religion and its world.
O Lord, hasten its repentance for it, and wash its sins with the water of piety!
If You, my Master, chastise it, who then can hope for its mercy?
So be kind to it and forgive its sin — You are its Creator and its Master.

THE POEM IN TĀʾ:
By the light of whose face You have manifested, Your holiness has stunned my bewilderment; and in You, though nothing is hidden from You, is my perplexity.
O You who are the nearest of things to every glance, You are the farthest thing from every vision!
You appeared, and when You dazzled by Your manifestation, You became hidden with a hiddenness that nearly destroyed my cloak.
You cast between intellect and sense, when You were hidden, a disagreement that no reconciliation can remove.
When the intellect claims Your existence, denying to sense what it negates, it says to it: "Stand firm!"
For sense negates You as a form it sees, while the intellect is satisfied with You by proof.
From here arises the origin of the disagreement, and concord is difficult due to a difference in the demand of nature.
If you say: "I do not see You in every form I see," the eye of my insight rejects that.
And if you say: "I do see You," my words are denied, and my eye does not testify to that.
You manifested Yourself from me in me, so You appeared to me; You hid with a hiddenness too subtle for every thought.
Yet there remained no mountain that saw Your manifestation to me but it was shattered by a thunderbolt.
And You whispered to me in my secret from me, so I became, having folded away from all other than You my folding.
There is no room in me for other than You to occur to me; my time in You is non-temporal.
The deposit of the Holy Spirit is your soul — return it, for returning the deposit is among the duties of the intellect.
And its return is only by perfecting it with what befits it, of the acquisition of every virtue.
Whenever it manifests from the turbidities of the world of nature, it heals a substance and manifests.
I have advised you with my utmost effort — if you accept, then do not carry advice under the rule of deceit.
And the limit of my power I have said; but your acceptance is not within the capacity of my power.
And how can one be made happy whose lot was already written by a pen in the Tablet, one day, as misery?
The youth thinks the pleasures of his world are a blessing — but they are nothing but a punishment in truth.
His ignorance reaches what no enemy reaches with the edge of the sword at the moment of opportunity.
So guard your soul and protect it, for its happiness lies in the doing of every hardship.
And oppose its passion as much as you can, for it is its enemy, seeking for it every calamity.
By my life, I have warned with the warning of one who is compassionate, and I have exceeded in clarification the limit of a testament.
So rise, strive, ascend, and exert yourself, and seek absolutely, with your hand, against what is in you — the worst of deeds.
For you are of a radiant light and a darkness, by what is in you of body and precious soul.
The body governs life, and it is governed by what is in you of guarded secrets of knowledge.
So you are either a stoned Satan or an angel, by what you practice of ugly deed and chastity.
Truly, I have in the soul a preoccupation from me; by it my angelic state is completed while I endure.
The doubt of accidents was cleared from me by an intuition, kindled like a lamp in my substance.
I saw by it the Divine Light shining behind veils of subtle matters.
So I verified what I had been doubting, and I witnessed what had been hidden in a secret.
And I grasped what is intended from my beginning, and what is meant by my living, my dying, and my return.
By the mirror of the soul, there shone to me in its polish, facing the two worlds, every reality.
And no doubt remained in me of what people had concealed in many matters.
The soul cast its staff from me, and I was certain that my journey, when it unveiled, was the unveiling of my success.
What I have said is indicated by the state of sleep, when sensation is stilled in you by slumber.
And the tablet of the unseen faces the soul, just as a mirror faces another polished mirror.
So what is in the tablet is imprinted in the soul; thus it is, from there, by knowledge of the unseen, a copy of my copy.
If abstraction were possible in every wakefulness, you would witness, not in sleep, every wonder.
And what is with God is not like Adam, nor is this one's sin related to that one's sin.
And he foolishly hopes to enter Paradise, and to envy himself therein with every envy —
Contrary to what analogy gives, and the intellect, without transmission, has not established for him a proof of argument.
Does he come out of it — Adam, for the sin of a slip — and this one enter it for every slip he does?
And how do you see the Generous One judging by a lapse, and drawing near the vile, base one with every predicament?
Were it not for a hadith on intercession that has come, and the interpretation of verses to console the lonely,
No soul would hope to win Paradise if it were not purified of every sin.
And yet the disagreement of people in this is apparent; clear proofs are established upon it.
And since the disagreement is established, it is obligatory upon every possessor of intellect to adhere to dissimulation (taqiyyah).
And to abandon deceptive hopes, after seeing in his father Adam every lesson.
And if the evil-doer were not requited for his deed, nor the good-doer, the affairs of creation would be wasted.
And there would be no wisdom in the living and the dying, and the rule of every law would be impossible.
And remote is the revival of our living and our dying in vain, without a meaning in which is the secret of the will.
Is it good that lofty palaces be built in the finest arrangements and most beautiful structure,
Then demolished into nothingness for no meaning? Indeed, that is ugly to sound intellects.
That is a thing done in vain, and this universe is not governed by vanity.
So nothing remains but that its affair is governed by a Clement One, encompassing in knowledge, just in judgment.
No soul that obeyed Him in fear has been wretched, and no soul that disobeyed Him in desire has been happy.
But by the light of knowledge this one is saved, and that one is destroyed by ignorance — the ugliest destruction.
So how wondrous is one who seeks for his soul deliverance, yet does not turn away from it for a sin!
And one who repents of a humiliation, yet no tears are seen from him like the mouths of pouring clouds!
And one who is informed that God's power does not incapacitate him, yet he does not fear the onset of vengeance!
And one upon whose mirror of intellect the lights have shone, over the darknesses of nature from him manifested,
And the planting of the intellect in the heart has borne fruit, for the seeker of modesty, the ugliness of every vice.
And no soul has reached the world of purity without what is below the acquisition of the clear sciences,
And its distinction from its kind by cognitions that circulate it in the world of humanity.
And the drop may fill the vessel, and it fills with water until there is no increase for a drop.
So You brought me out of myself by admitting a trial, and made me desolate of myself by the intimacy of love.
And You gave me to drink from the wine of Your love a draught; my intoxication by it remains until the day of my resurrection.
